claim: CRISPR-Cas9 genome engineering has revolutionised high-throughput functional genomic screens.
source: CRISPR-Cas9 genome engineering has revolutionised high-throughput functional genomic screens.
evidence: This is a general statement about the impact of CRISPR-Cas9 technology, drawing from established scientific consensus in the field.

claim: Recent work has raised concerns regarding the performance of CRISPR-Cas9 screens using TP53 wild-type human cells due to a p53-mediated DNA damage response limiting the efficiency of generating viable edited cells.
source: However, recent work has raised concerns regarding the performance of CRISPR-Cas9 screens using TP53 wild-type human cells due to a p53-mediated DNA damage response (DDR) limiting the efficiency of generating viable edited cells.
evidence: This claim references recent work in the field, supported by citations in the introduction section (Haapaniemi et al., 2018; Ihry et al., 2018).

claim: Functional p53 status negatively affects identification of significantly depleted genes in CRISPR-Cas9 screens.
source: Our work demonstrates that although functional p53 status negatively affects identification of significantly depleted genes, optimal screen design can nevertheless enable robust screen performance.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the authors' experimental work comparing wild-type and TP53 knockout cells.

claim: Optimal screen design can enable robust CRISPR-Cas9 screen performance despite functional p53 status.
source: Our work demonstrates that although functional p53 status negatively affects identification of significantly depleted genes, optimal screen design can nevertheless enable robust screen performance.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion from the authors' experimental data and analysis.

claim: Pooled CRISPR-Cas9 cell viability screens have been successfully employed in determining gene essentiality.
source: Pooled CRISPR-Cas9 cell viability screens have been successfully employed in determining gene essentiality (Hart et al., 2015), identifying genetic interactions (Chan et al., 2019) and assessing drug sensitivities across various genetic backgrounds (Han et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hart et al., 2015.

claim: Pooled CRISPR-Cas9 cell viability screens have been successfully employed in identifying genetic interactions.
source: Pooled CRISPR-Cas9 cell viability screens have been successfully employed in determining gene essentiality (Hart et al., 2015), identifying genetic interactions (Chan et al., 2019) and assessing drug sensitivities across various genetic backgrounds (Han et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Chan et al., 2019.

claim: Pooled CRISPR-Cas9 cell viability screens have been successfully employed in assessing drug sensitivities across various genetic backgrounds.
source: Pooled CRISPR-Cas9 cell viability screens have been successfully employed in determining gene essentiality (Hart et al., 2015), identifying genetic interactions (Chan et al., 2019) and assessing drug sensitivities across various genetic backgrounds (Han et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Han et al., 2017.

claim: Recent reports concerning technical difficulties in CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing in p53-proficient cells have brought into question the suitability of p53-proficient cell lines for high throughput CRISPR-Cas9 genetic screens.
source: In particular, recent reports concerning technical difficulties in CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing in p53-proficient cells, have brought into question the suitability of p53-proficient cell lines for high throughput CRISPR-Cas9 genetic screens (Haapaniemi et al., 2018; Ihry et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Haapaniemi et al., 2018 and Ihry et al., 2018.

claim: TP53 acts as a master regulator of cell-cycle checkpoint activation.
source: TP53, encoding p53, acts as a master regulator of cell-cycle checkpoint activation (Kastan et al., 1991), cellular senescence (Shay et al., 1991) and induction of apoptosis in response to DNA damage (Clarke et al., 1993; Lowe et al., 1993; Lakin and Jackson, 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kastan et al., 1991.

claim: TP53 acts as a master regulator of cellular senescence.
source: TP53, encoding p53, acts as a master regulator of cell-cycle checkpoint activation (Kastan et al., 1991), cellular senescence (Shay et al., 1991) and induction of apoptosis in response to DNA damage (Clarke et al., 1993; Lowe et al., 1993; Lakin and Jackson, 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Shay et al., 1991.

claim: TP53 acts as a master regulator of induction of apoptosis in response to DNA damage.
source: TP53, encoding p53, acts as a master regulator of cell-cycle checkpoint activation (Kastan et al., 1991), cellular senescence (Shay et al., 1991) and induction of apoptosis in response to DNA damage (Clarke et al., 1993; Lowe et al., 1993; Lakin and Jackson, 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Clarke et al., 1993; Lowe et al., 1993; Lakin and Jackson, 1999.

claim: TP53 is the most important tumour suppressor gene, with loss of function mutations in up to 50% of human cancers.
source: TP53 is arguably the most important tumour suppressor gene, with loss of function mutations in up to 50% of human cancers (Bouaoun et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Bouaoun et al., 2016.

claim: Generation of DNA double strand breaks induces p53-dependent cell-cycle arrest in normal fibroblasts.
source: Generation of DNA double strand breaks (DSBs) induces p53-dependent cell-cycle arrest in normal fibroblasts (Di Leonardo et al., 1994), and most CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing approaches rely on DSB generation to achieve efficient editing (Jinek et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Di Leonardo et al., 1994.

claim: Most CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing approaches rely on DSB generation to achieve efficient editing.
source: Generation of DNA double strand breaks (DSBs) induces p53-dependent cell-cycle arrest in normal fibroblasts (Di Leonardo et al., 1994), and most CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing approaches rely on DSB generation to achieve efficient editing (Jinek et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Jinek et al., 2012.

claim: CRISPR-Cas9-associated DSBs in hPSCs induce a p53-mediated apoptotic response, leading to high levels of toxicity and reduced editing efficiency.
source: Recent work has shown that CRISPR-Cas9-associated DSBs in hPSCs (human pluripotent stem cells) induce a p53-mediated apoptotic response, leading to high levels of toxicity and reduced editing efficiency in this background (Ihry et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ihry et al., 2018.

claim: A p53-mediated DSB response in wild-type RPE-1 cells severely impaired identification of essential genes in a CRISPR-Cas9 screen when compared to RPE-1 TP53KO cells.
source: Furthermore, a similar p53-mediated DSB response in wild-type retinal pigment epithelial (RPE-1) cells reportedly severely impaired identification of essential genes in a CRISPR-Cas9 screen when compared to RPE-1 TP53 knockout (TP53KO) cells (Haapaniemi et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Haapaniemi et al., 2018.

claim: Analysis of data from a small number of additional screens in p53 wild-type RPE-1 cells has shown that performance of successful CRISPR screens is possible in this cellular background.
source: In contrast, analysis of data from a small number of additional screens in p53 wild-type RPE-1 cells has shown that performance of successful CRISPR screens, as determined by essential gene identification and enrichment of expected targets, is possible in this cellular background (Brown et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Brown et al., 2019.

claim: The authors carried out parallel CRISPR-Cas9 screens in wild-type and TP53KO RPE-1 cells with two independent Cas9-expressing monoclonal populations for each genetic background.
source: We carried out parallel screens, in wild-type and TP53KO RPE-1 cells with two independent Cas9-expressing monoclonal populations for each genetic background, selected based on p53 status and high Cas9 cutting efficiency (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design performed by the authors.

claim: The authors designed a bespoke dual guide RNA library targeting 852 DDR-related genes, with 112 olfactory receptor genes included as non-essential gene controls and 14 sequence-scrambled negative controls.
source: To facilitate high screen sensitivity and in-depth interrogation of p53-mediated responses to CRISPR-Cas9-associated DSBs, we designed a bespoke dual guide RNA library targeting 852 DDR-related genes, with 112 olfactory receptor genes included as non-essential gene controls and 14 sequence-scrambled negative controls (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design and materials used by the authors.

claim: The smaller size of the custom library compared to a whole genome library enabled high guide representation (>1000 x) to be maintained throughout the screen.
source: Moreover, the smaller size of this library compared to a whole genome library enabled high guide representation (>1000 x) to be maintained throughout the screen, minimising the impact of this key factor on screen sensitivity (Miles et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design with citation to Miles et al., 2016 for the importance of guide representation.

claim: High guide representation minimises the impact on screen sensitivity.
source: Moreover, the smaller size of this library compared to a whole genome library enabled high guide representation (>1000 x) to be maintained throughout the screen, minimising the impact of this key factor on screen sensitivity (Miles et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Miles et al., 2016.

claim: The dual guide RNA vector design increases the frequency of functional knockout events in transduced cells compared to the canonical single guide RNA approach.
source: In addition, our library incorporated a dual guide RNA vector design (Erard et al., 2017) to increase the frequency of functional knockout events in transduced cells compared to the canonical single guide RNA (sgRNA) approach.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Erard et al., 2017 and describes the rationale for the experimental design.

claim: Depletion of core essential genes was clearly evident in both wild-type and TP53KO backgrounds.
source: In our screens, depletion of core essential genes (as defined by Hart et al., 2017) was clearly evident in both wild-type and TP53KO backgrounds (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the authors' experimental data, shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The TP53KO screen slightly outperformed the wild-type screen at both harvesting timepoints in terms of detection of essential genes by rank.
source: Nevertheless, the TP53KO screen slightly outperformed the wild-type screen at both harvesting timepoints in terms of detection of essential genes by rank.
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' analysis of their experimental data, supported by the ROC curve analysis mentioned in the text.

claim: Essential genes were much more likely to have low adjusted p-values (q-values) in the TP53KO background, compared to wild-type.
source: When the significance of gene depletions was considered, we found that essential genes were much more likely to have low adjusted p-values (q-values) in the TP53KO background, compared to wild-type.
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' analysis of their experimental data.

claim: The day 19 timepoint outperformed the day 15 timepoint, detecting increased numbers of essential genes at a given significance threshold.
source: In addition, we observed that the day 19 timepoint outperformed the day 15 timepoint, detecting increased numbers of essential genes at a given significance threshold (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' analysis of their experimental data, shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Log fold changes across non-core essential genes were not significantly different between the two genetic backgrounds (p=0.60).
source: While log fold changes (LFCs) across non-core essential ('not essential') genes were not significantly different between the two genetic backgrounds (p=0.60), LFCs for core essential genes were significantly lower in the TP53KO screens compared to screens in TP53 wild-type settings (p=0.0010) (Figure 2D), consistent with wild-type cells initiating a p53-mediated response to Cas9-induced DSBs.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the authors' analysis of their experimental data, shown in Figure 2D.

claim: LFCs for core essential genes were significantly lower in the TP53KO screens compared to screens in TP53 wild-type settings (p=0.0010).
source: While log fold changes (LFCs) across non-core essential ('not essential') genes were not significantly different between the two genetic backgrounds (p=0.60), LFCs for core essential genes were significantly lower in the TP53KO screens compared to screens in TP53 wild-type settings (p=0.0010) (Figure 2D), consistent with wild-type cells initiating a p53-mediated response to Cas9-induced DSBs.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the authors' analysis of their experimental data, shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Wild-type cells initiate a p53-mediated response to Cas9-induced DSBs that inhibits the proliferation rates of all transduced cells during the course of the screens.
source: This would inhibit the proliferation rates of all transduced cells during the course of the screens, leading to smaller LFCs and a narrower distribution of guides within the population, with a consequent reduction in genes with significant depletion scores.
evidence: This is an inference from the authors' experimental data to explain the observed differences in LFCs.

claim: In TP53 wild-type cells, guides targeting TP53 were the most significantly enriched.
source: As expected, in TP53 wild-type cells, guides targeting TP53 were the most significantly enriched, with guides targeting other components of the p53 pathway showing the most significant differences between the two genetic backgrounds.
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' analysis of their experimental data.

claim: Guides targeting CDKN1A were significantly enriched in the TP53 wild-type background.
source: Guides significantly enriched in the TP53 wild-type background included those targeting CDKN1A that encodes p21, the major downstream mediator of p53-mediated cell cycle arrest (el-Deiry et al., 1993), and those targeting USP28 that encodes a deubiquitylating enzyme that acts to stabilise p53 (Zhang et al., 2006; Cuella-Martin et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' experimental data, with citation to el-Deiry et al., 1993 for the function of CDKN1A/p21.

claim: CDKN1A encodes p21, the major downstream mediator of p53-mediated cell cycle arrest.
source: Guides significantly enriched in the TP53 wild-type background included those targeting CDKN1A that encodes p21, the major downstream mediator of p53-mediated cell cycle arrest (el-Deiry et al., 1993), and those targeting USP28 that encodes a deubiquitylating enzyme that acts to stabilise p53 (Zhang et al., 2006; Cuella-Martin et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to el-Deiry et al., 1993.

claim: Guides targeting USP28 were significantly enriched in the TP53 wild-type background.
source: Guides significantly enriched in the TP53 wild-type background included those targeting CDKN1A that encodes p21, the major downstream mediator of p53-mediated cell cycle arrest (el-Deiry et al., 1993), and those targeting USP28 that encodes a deubiquitylating enzyme that acts to stabilise p53 (Zhang et al., 2006; Cuella-Martin et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' experimental data, with citations to Zhang et al., 2006 and Cuella-Martin et al., 2016 for the function of USP28.

claim: USP28 encodes a deubiquitylating enzyme that acts to stabilise p53.
source: Guides significantly enriched in the TP53 wild-type background included those targeting CDKN1A that encodes p21, the major downstream mediator of p53-mediated cell cycle arrest (el-Deiry et al., 1993), and those targeting USP28 that encodes a deubiquitylating enzyme that acts to stabilise p53 (Zhang et al., 2006; Cuella-Martin et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Zhang et al., 2006 and Cuella-Martin et al., 2016.

claim: Guides targeting MDM2 and MDM4 were significantly depleted in the wild-type but not the TP53 knockout background.
source: In contrast, guides targeting genes that were significantly depleted in the wild-type but not the TP53 knockout background included MDM2 and MDM4, which act as negative regulators of p53.
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' experimental data.

claim: MDM2 is an E3 ubiquitin ligase that targets p53 for degradation.
source: MDM2 is an E3 ubiquitin ligase that targets p53 for degradation (Haupt et al., 1997), while MDM4 inhibits p53-dependent transcriptional activity (Francoz et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Haupt et al., 1997.

claim: MDM4 inhibits p53-dependent transcriptional activity.
source: MDM2 is an E3 ubiquitin ligase that targets p53 for degradation (Haupt et al., 1997), while MDM4 inhibits p53-dependent transcriptional activity (Francoz et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Francoz et al., 2006.

claim: SETDB1 was enriched in the TP53 wild-type background.
source: SETDB1, which acts via MDM2, was also enriched in the TP53 wild-type background.
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' experimental data.

claim: SETDB1 forms a complex with p53 and catalyses p53 K370 di-methylation.
source: This protein forms a complex with p53 and catalyses p53 K370 di-methylation. Attenuation of SETDB1 reduces the level of di-methylation at this site, leading to increased recognition and degradation of p53 by MDM2 (Fei et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Fei et al., 2015.

claim: Attenuation of SETDB1 reduces the level of di-methylation at p53 K370, leading to increased recognition and degradation of p53 by MDM2.
source: This protein forms a complex with p53 and catalyses p53 K370 di-methylation. Attenuation of SETDB1 reduces the level of di-methylation at this site, leading to increased recognition and degradation of p53 by MDM2 (Fei et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Fei et al., 2015.

claim: Cell cycle and p53 signalling were the two pathways that were enriched when assessing enrichment/depletion of specific biological pathways between the wild-type and TP53KO backgrounds.
source: Furthermore, when we assessed the enrichment/depletion of specific biological pathways between the wild-type and TP53KO backgrounds, cell cycle and p53 signalling were the two pathways that were enriched (Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' pathway analysis of their experimental data, shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: EP300 was enriched on both genetic backgrounds.
source: EP300 was enriched on both genetic backgrounds and has an established role as a tumour suppressor through the regulation of the G1/S cell-cycle transition (Ait-Si-Ali et al., 2000).
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' experimental data, with citation to Ait-Si-Ali et al., 2000 for the function of EP300.

claim: EP300 has an established role as a tumour suppressor through the regulation of the G1/S cell-cycle transition.
source: EP300 was enriched on both genetic backgrounds and has an established role as a tumour suppressor through the regulation of the G1/S cell-cycle transition (Ait-Si-Ali et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ait-Si-Ali et al., 2000.

claim: CCNA2 was depleted on both genetic backgrounds.
source: CCNA2, or cyclin A2, was depleted on both genetic backgrounds as it interacts with both CDK1 and CDK2 to drive S-phase progression and regulate the G1/S and G2/M phases of the cell-cycle (Pagano et al., 1992).
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' experimental data, with citation to Pagano et al., 1992 for the function of CCNA2.

claim: CCNA2 interacts with both CDK1 and CDK2 to drive S-phase progression and regulate the G1/S and G2/M phases of the cell-cycle.
source: CCNA2, or cyclin A2, was depleted on both genetic backgrounds as it interacts with both CDK1 and CDK2 to drive S-phase progression and regulate the G1/S and G2/M phases of the cell-cycle (Pagano et al., 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Pagano et al., 1992.

claim: Biologically meaningful enrichment and depletion analyses at the individual gene and pathway levels can be performed in TP53 wild-type settings despite reduced screen sensitivity.
source: Altogether, these results demonstrate that despite reduced screen sensitivity in p53-proficient cells, biologically meaningful enrichment and depletion analyses at the individual gene and pathway levels can, when required, still be performed in TP53 wild-type settings.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the authors' experimental data and analysis.

claim: The performance of all screens was similar, with the exception of Haapaniemi et al. (2018) data which underperformed in the ability to distinguish essential genes.
source: When we performed a comparative ROC curve analysis to assess the screens' abilities to discriminate between core essential genes and other genes (Figure 3A), this established that the performance of all screens was similar, with the exception of Haapaniemi et al. (2018) data which underperformed in the ability to distinguish essential genes.
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' comparative analysis of multiple screen datasets, shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Core essential genes formed distributions distinct from those of olfactory receptors and other non-essential genes in all wild-type screens, with the exception of the Haapaniemi et al. screen where the separation was minimal.
source: This revealed that the core essential genes formed distributions distinct from those of olfactory receptors and other non-essential genes in all wild-type screens, with the exception of the Haapaniemi et al. screen where the separation was minimal (the smaller median LFC in our screen compared to the other four successful screens did not notably hinder our ability to distinguish essential genes).
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' analysis of LFC distributions across multiple screen datasets.

claim: CRISPR-Cas9 screens can be performed successfully in a p53-proficient background.
source: Taken together, these analyses provide further evidence that CRISPR-Cas9 screens can be performed successfully in a p53-proficient background.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the authors' comparative analysis of multiple screen datasets.

claim: The Haapaniemi et al. screen is an outlier in its inability to robustly detect essential genes, possibly due to differences in experimental design and execution.
source: It appears that the Haapaniemi et al. screen is an outlier in its inability to robustly detect essential genes, possibly due to differences in experimental design and execution, and perhaps reflecting relatively low editing efficiency of the polyclonal RPE-1 population used in this screen.
evidence: This is an inference from the authors' comparative analysis, speculating on reasons for the poor performance of the Haapaniemi et al. screen.

claim: The variance in LFC between guides targeting the same gene is less in the authors' screen than in other screens.
source: Figure 3C shows that the variance in LFC between guides targeting the same gene is less in our screen than in these other screens.
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The decrease in variance in LFC is linked to the much higher gRNA representation kept throughout the authors' screen (>1000 x mean gRNA representation) than in other screens.
source: We speculate that this decrease in variance is linked to the much higher gRNA representation kept throughout our screen (>1000 x mean gRNA representation) than in these other screens, although we cannot discard the possibility that the dual-sgRNA system we used is the cause of this effect.
evidence: This is speculation by the authors about the cause of the observed decrease in variance.

claim: High gRNA representation is relevant for the success and reliability of CRISPR-Cas9 screens.
source: High gRNA representation is relevant for the success and reliability of CRISPR-Cas9 screens, with most published recommendations suggesting screening to at least 200x gRNA representation (Aregger et al., 2019) but ideally >500 x (Joung et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Aregger et al., 2019 and Joung et al., 2017.

claim: Most published recommendations suggest screening to at least 200x gRNA representation.
source: High gRNA representation is relevant for the success and reliability of CRISPR-Cas9 screens, with most published recommendations suggesting screening to at least 200x gRNA representation (Aregger et al., 2019) but ideally >500 x (Joung et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Aregger et al., 2019.

claim: Ideally, gRNA representation should be >500x.
source: High gRNA representation is relevant for the success and reliability of CRISPR-Cas9 screens, with most published recommendations suggesting screening to at least 200x gRNA representation (Aregger et al., 2019) but ideally >500 x (Joung et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Joung et al., 2017.

claim: The MSKCC screen is the only dataset to show a distribution with a substantial number of zero reads in the final samples.
source: The MSKCC screen is the only dataset to show a distribution with a substantial number of zero reads in the final samples, which accounts for the decreased variance at more negative LFCs in this screen (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Low read counts can notably decrease screen sensitivity.
source: Through modelling the effect of decreased sequencing depth in our data, we demonstrate that low read counts can notably decrease screen sensitivity (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' modeling analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: A p53-mediated response negatively impacts the sensitivity of CRISPR-Cas9 screens.
source: In summary, we present data from parallel screens in TP53 wild-type and TP53KO RPE-1 cells, which demonstrate that a p53-mediated response does negatively impact the sensitivity of CRISPR-Cas9 screens.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion from the authors' experimental data.

claim: The extent of the impact of TP53 status on CRISPR-Cas9 screens might vary depending on the cell type being studied.
source: The extent of the impact of TP53 status on CRISPR-Cas9 screens might vary depending on the cell type being studied, including those with loss-of-function mutations in TP53 without being fully TP53 null.
evidence: This is speculation by the authors about the generalizability of their findings.

claim: Most or all cell lines with an intact TP53 pathway and proper cell-cycle checkpoint activation would likely recapitulate the authors' findings.
source: However, we anticipate that most or all cell lines with an intact TP53 pathway and proper cell-cycle checkpoint activation would likely recapitulate our findings.
evidence: This is speculation by the authors about the generalizability of their findings.

claim: Important factors impacting sensitivity include the guide RNA library used, the magnitude of guide effects, adequate gRNA representation and sufficient sequencing depth.
source: Other important factors impacting sensitivity include the guide RNA library used, the magnitude of guide effects, adequate gRNA representation and sufficient sequencing depth.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the authors' analysis of their own and published screen data.

claim: Selection of high-editing efficiency Cas9-expressing cells is highly recommended.
source: Selection of high-editing efficiency Cas9-expressing cells is also highly recommended and use of biological replicates enables identification of clonal variation.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the authors' experimental design and analysis.

claim: Use of biological replicates enables identification of clonal variation.
source: Selection of high-editing efficiency Cas9-expressing cells is also highly recommended and use of biological replicates enables identification of clonal variation.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the authors' experimental design.

claim: Considering key factors in screen design and execution allows successful CRISPR-Cas9 screens to be carried out in both p53-proficient and p53-deficient cells.
source: Considering these factors in screen design and execution allows successful CRISPR-Cas9 screens to be carried out in both p53-proficient and p53-deficient cells, thereby fostering new biological insights.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion from the authors' work.

claim: The custom dual-sgRNA library targets a total of 95 core essential genes.
source: The genes targeted by this library include a total of 95 core essential genes.
evidence: This is a description of the library composition used in the experiments.

claim: Cells were infected at a low multiplicity of infection (MOI=0.3).
source: Cells were infected at a low multiplicity of infection (MOI=0.3).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental method, shown in Figure 1.

claim: An initial sample was harvested 48 hours after infection.
source: An initial sample was harvested 48 hours after infection.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental method, shown in Figure 1.

claim: Transduced cells were selected with puromycin and harvested at days 15 and 19.
source: Subsequently, transduced cells were selected with puromycin and harvested at days 15 and 19.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental method, shown in Figure 1.

claim: MAGeCK was used to determine the relative depletion and enrichment of genes in later samples compared to the 48-hour samples.
source: MAGeCK (Li et al., 2014) was used to determine the relative depletion and enrichment of genes in later samples compared to the 48-hour samples.
evidence: This is a description of the data analysis method, shown in Figure 1 and cited to Li et al., 2014.

claim: RPE-1 wild-type cells were originally obtained from the ATCC cell repository by Professor Jonathon Pines.
source: RPE-1 wild-type cells were originally obtained from the ATCC cell repository by Professor Jonathon Pines.
evidence: This is a description of the cell line source.

claim: RPE-1 cells were routinely tested for mycoplasma and were authenticated using Affymetrix SNP6 copy number analysis.
source: They were routinely tested for mycoplasma and were authenticated using Affymetrix SNP6 copy number analysis.
evidence: This is a description of quality control measures for the cell lines.

claim: RPE-1 TP53KO cells were generated as described previously by Chiang et al., 2016.
source: RPE-1 TP53KO cells were generated as described previously (Chiang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a description of the cell line generation method, supported by citation to Chiang et al., 2016.
